title: Playing 'When the Saints' and why musicians tire of it
summary: Saints is played; Allen says northern musicians call it the monster and that the spirit matters more than the tune.

bands.name: Johnny Wiggs and His New Orleans Kings

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience

I'll stick by that guy instead of forcing Johnny to. We get so tired of hearing that. You know, the northern musicians call that the monster because people request it over and over again. And they think that New Orleans jazz consists of ten tunes, the five most popular of which are when the saints go marching in. That isn't the thing. That isn't the thing. It's the spirit behind it. It's the spirit behind it and the man behind it. When New Orleans jazz is played under the right circumstances, it can be when the saints go marching in. Or it can be a popular song like My Melancholy Baby or the blues like Congo Square was. It's what you put into it, your feelings. And, of course, the crowd helps. If you're playing when the saints go marching in at a funeral, it has a special meaning. And if you're playing it at a party where people are dancing and having a good time, to me it sounds better than. But if the same person requests it thirteen times in a row, it gets all the time out of it. So do I.
